+

+def _run_table(s, table):
+    """
+    Apply every replacement of a _replace_table to s, in order. present is a
+    superset of the characters of s (a minted token is added once it was
+    produced), so a pair with a character outside it cannot occur in s and
+    its replace would be a no-op: it is skipped without scanning s.
+    """
+    present = set(s)
+    add = present.add
+    for ps, c, a, b in table:
+        if a in present and b in present:
+            t = s.replace(ps, c)
+            if t is not s:
+                add(c)
+                s = t
+    return s

The required ratio is 0.99. The library's encode and train paths are already heavily optimised and seem to be only a small share of the measured instructions, so I don't have a change that reaches the 1% minimum. journal.text:
I read basic.py, regex.py, base.py and lineage_bench.py, then searched for _replace_table, _chunk_table and enc_state[4] to see how the replace path is wired. My idea was to skip replaces whose pair characters cannot occur in the string, checked against a set of the string's characters. I edited basic.py and regex.py in several small passes.

My one sandbox evaluation built fine on both sides and gave identical outputs, but it was rejected for no improvement. encode_ir went from 423530685 to 425068500, ratio 1.0036. train_ir went from 365691233 to 366322208, ratio 1.0017. The required ratio was 0.9900. I gave up and submitted no candidate.

I now think encode and train are already heavily optimised. The character-set check costs more than the replaces it skips. Those paths also seem to be a small share of the measured instructions.

Next time I should first find where the bulk of the measured instructions go, outside the encode and train loops, before touching the replace logic again.
